note: research/m01-classic-rpg was not on origin when this file was written. These records are self-verified fetches by Agent 06. They use the SELF-06 prefix so they cannot be mistaken for another agent's INS-0X ids. Facts below are only what the fetched page stated. If Agent 01 later publishes the same creature, prefer their inspirationId.

inspirations.name: Slime (Dragon Quest)
facts: Slimes are a fictional species of slime monster in the Dragon Quest series, conceived as a weak and common enemy for the 1986 game and inspired by Wizardry.

Yuji Horii said the slime was originally conceived as a pile of goo. Akira Toriyama's design came back as a teardrop, which the team considered perfect, and that teardrop became the series mascot and merchandise.

sources.title: Slime (Dragon Quest)
sources.supports: Both facts are in the lead and in the Concept and design section fetched the same day.

inspirations.parodyPotential: Use the weak common blob. Do not draw the teardrop mascot.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: The teardrop design is a living franchise mascot. The pile-of-goo concept is the usable distance.

inspirations.name: Mimic (Dungeons & Dragons)
facts: In Dungeons & Dragons the mimic is a monster that changes shape to look like an inanimate object, commonly a chest. It was introduced in the original Monster Manual (1977) and is described there as a subterranean creature that cannot stand sunlight and can mimic stone or wood, posing as stonework, doors, or chests.
The same article describes a powerful adhesive and pseudopods. Those two mechanics are specific to this game monster and are not used in the parody.

sources.title: Mimic (Dungeons & Dragons)
sources.supports: Chest disguise, 1977 debut, sunlight aversion, stone-or-wood mimicry, and the adhesive pseudopods.

inspirations.parodyPotential: An object that argues about being claimed. Not a wooden chest, and not the adhesive fight.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Iconic game monster. The chest silhouette plus a tongue would be too close.

inspirations.name: Animated object
inspirations.origin: Folklore and fantasy stories, including games
facts: An animated object is an item that acts on its own, apart from a person using it, often by supernatural means.
The article says forms ranging from household tools to armor have appeared in stories throughout history, and that animated objects also appear in games.

sources.title: Animated object
sources.supports: Self-moving items, including armor, in stories and in games.

inspirations.parodyPotential: Empty armor that clocks in at the wrong size.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: The page is a broad survey, not a single bestiary entry. Confidence stays medium. The Japanese tsukumogami paragraph on the same page is a different tradition and is not the source for the armor parody.

inspirations.name: Goblin
facts: A goblin is a small, often malevolent humanoid in European folklore, mischievous, furry or leathery, and sometimes said to shapeshift. The article says they are often depicted with green skin.
They are said to live underground or in households and to range from pranks to much worse harm. The word is also used as a blanket term for small fay creatures.

sources.title: Goblin
sources.supports: Small household or underground trickster, leathery or furry, and the modern green-skin depiction.

inspirations.parodyPotential: A household clerk with fangs. Not a green game goblin.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Folklore type. Green skin plus a game silhouette would collide with living game goblins. Do not play the harmful end of the range as comedy.

inspirations.name: Phoenix (mythology)
facts: The phoenix is a legendary immortal bird that cyclically regenerates. The article places its origin in Greek mythology and notes analogues in other cultures.
It is associated with the sun and obtains new life by rising from the ashes of its predecessor. Some legends have it die in a show of flames; others have it burn, decompose, and be born again.

sources.title: Phoenix (mythology)
sources.supports: Cyclic rebirth from ashes, Greek origin, and the flame death.

inspirations.parodyPotential: The bow is grand and the next body is a sooty hen. Not a game summon.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Do not use an Egyptian sacred-bird costume or a franchise phoenix.

inspirations.name: Spring-heeled Jack
facts: Spring-heeled Jack is a Victorian English folklore entity. The first claimed sighting was in 1837, with later reports especially in suburban London, the Midlands, and Scotland. The stories emphasize extraordinary leaps.

Claimed descriptions include a frightening face, clawed hands, and eyes like red balls of fire. One report put a helmet and a tight white oilskin garment under a black cloak. Several reports add blue and white flames from the mouth and sharp metallic claws, and at least two people claimed he spoke English.

sources.title: Spring-heeled Jack
sources.supports: 1837 sightings, leaps, claws, fiery eyes, cloak and oilskin, and the flame reports.

inspirations.parodyPotential: The leap is terrifying until it is only someone skipping a queue.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Historical urban legend. Do not copy one penny-dreadful illustration as the costume.

inspirations.name: Troll
facts: A troll is a being in Nordic folklore, including Norse mythology.
In Old Norse sources, beings described as trolls live in isolated rocks, mountains, or caves, keep to small family units, and are rarely helpful.

sources.title: Troll
sources.supports: Isolated rock, mountain, or cave households, and the rarely-helpful note.

inspirations.parodyPotential: A household of one, filed under rock.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: The fetched lead does not mention a bridge toll. Do not add one.

inspirations.name: Jersey Devil
facts: The Jersey Devil, also called the Leeds Devil, is a cryptid of the New Jersey Pine Barrens in South Jersey, also told around Philadelphia.

A common description is a bipedal kangaroo-like or wyvern-like creature with a horse-like or goat-like head, bat-like wings, horns, small clawed arms, cloven hooves, and a forked tail, said to move quickly and to scream.

sources.title: Jersey Devil
sources.supports: Pine Barrens cryptid and the winged, hoofed, horse-or-goat-headed description.

inspirations.parodyPotential: Hooves and wings in a service corridor. Do not put Devil in the name.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: The word Devil in the folklore name is not a license to joke about religion. Leave it off the card.

inspirations.name: Robin Hood
facts: Robin Hood is a legendary English outlaw, a skilled archer. The oldest known versions make him a yeoman, not a noble.
He is traditionally depicted in Lincoln green. The article says he is today most closely associated with robbing the rich to give to the poor.

sources.title: Robin Hood
sources.supports: Yeoman outlaw, Lincoln green, and the rob-the-rich association.

inspirations.parodyPotential: He grabbed the wrong bag and is trying to give it back.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Do not copy a film's costume as the whole design.

inspirations.name: Flatwoods monster
facts: The Flatwoods monster is an alleged humanoid reported in Flatwoods, West Virginia, on 12 September 1952, after a bright light crossed the night sky.
In 2000, Joe Nickell suggested the light was a meteor and the creature may have been a barn owl in a tree, its shadow read as a large humanoid.

sources.title: Flatwoods monster
sources.supports: The 1952 report and the barn-owl explanation.

inspirations.parodyPotential: The shadow files a complaint against the write-up.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: Do not reproduce a famous illustration's exact head shape.

inspirations.name: Mandrake
facts: A mandrake is a toxic plant, chiefly Mediterranean Mandragora, whose roots are man-shaped and have been used in folk remedies.
Because the roots look like little people, and because the plants contain dangerous alkaloids, they have been tied to magic rituals.

sources.title: Mandrake
sources.supports: Man-shaped toxic root and the ritual association. The fetched text does not describe a scream.

inspirations.parodyPotential: A root that resents being a remedy. Do not add a scream the page did not state.
inspirations.sensitivityNote: The screaming mandrake is a later fiction image and is not in this source.
